summary_long: The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism Hollywood is sending a clear message: it's a friend of tech. Netflix is no longer a lone disruptor: historic studio MGM is now the property of Amazon's Jeff Bezos; David Ellison's takeover of Paramount and subsequent Warner Bros merger was supported by his tech giant father; and Apple TV has acted as a patron for multiple film-maker passion projects. Everyone, including trendy auteur-factory A24, is tying themselves financially to AI. The enormous pull of the tech industry – including its many trillions of dollars, oversized influence on politics and heavily pushed algorithms and AI products – means Hollywood is not alone in courting its wealth, but it has intensified the historic tension between art and commerce in the entertainment business. Technology that augments the human experience may be a compelling narrative subject, but this year brings a trio of films about the gurus responsible for the industry's false promises. summary_long: Decision follows independent review into handling of February ceremony, where his involuntary tics caused a BBC crisis John Davidson, the Tourette syndrome campaigner whose outburst at the British Academy film awards in February led to a crisis for Bafta (British Academy of Film and Television Arts) and the BBC , will attend the Bafta Scotland awards and watch the ceremony from a separate "relaxed" space. In a letter sent to Bafta members on Thursday, the organisation's chair Sara Putt and CEO Jane Millichip said that, after an independent review , Bafta had "strengthened and centralised our safeguarding, risk assessment and compliance processes" and had made arrangements in consultation with "safeguarding and inclusion experts" for Davidson's attendance at the awards ceremony organised by Bafta's Scottish branch, which is due to take place in November. summary_long: During the latest Weekend Ka Vaar episode of Bigg Boss , host Salman Khan asked Aamrapali Dubey to share her perspective on her equation with fellow contestants Love Gill and Scout, as well as the ongoing dynamics inside the house. Speaking about her bond with Love Gill, Aamrapali admitted that she sometimes feels protective of her and is affected by the way Love interacts with other contestants. She said, "I feel insecure when I see love with scout and Yung. If you are my number one, so make me feel like even I am your number one, but I feel that your number one is scout." Aamrapali further clarified that her reaction comes from a place of affection and protectiveness towards Love rather than simply being a result of insecurity. So, I don't like this quality of Love also, that when she gets angry, she forgets that respect towards the person." Agreeing with Aamrapali's observation, Salman Khan said, "yes, this is very correctly said, and I think Love should learn this from Aamrapali". If it happens once, yes, but this is a repeated pattern, which I don't support." Responding to her point, Salman said, "correct and if this issue is bought up here on weekend ka vaar that means it is being noticed by every one watching the show also." During the conversation, Aamrapali also shared her perspective on Qazi and addressed her stand on the Lollipop comment, which was also brought up by Salman Khan during the episode. summary_long: Docufictional 1981 comedy captures the working-class ska-pop pranksters in their hungry years with an almost Loachian authenticity Opting for the former is the best idea for this unexpectedly revealing, vividly atmospheric, often funny and alarming, docufictional comedy from 1981 about the rise of the baggy-trousered ska-pop national treasures Madness. It takes us from their beginnings in 1976 to their chart breakthrough: gormless, penniless blokes, obsessing about music and roaming north London's gritty districts of Camden Town, Stoke Newington and Crouch End. (This elicits some droll dialogue: "They're all the same, these streets" … "That's why they put signs on them.") Our naughty, dodgy heroes play people's parties, sign on the dole and do mortifying odd jobs, get told off by site foremen and office supervisors, drive to gigs in Arthur Daley vans, almost get into fights with skinheads and have calamitous arguments with the drummer during rehearsals. It could have carried on like that indefinitely, but the arrival of Graham "Suggs" McPherson as singer is the mysterious ingredient around which everything coalesces: his voice miraculously ups the band's game, apparently curing their worrying propensity for playing flat. His vocals mesh with the reggae thump of the keyboards and sax and the rest of the band's goofy jogging-on-the-spot stage energy. Continue reading...

summary_long: A daring, rich and funny study of the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self amid confounding changes Carol Morley's self-portrait of the artist as a young woman is rich, tender and terribly funny and sad: a study in the chaos of being young and a triptych of childhood, girlhood and youth, with some daring touches of Terence Davies. It is about the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self, even as the things you thought permanent suddenly collapse – including the background stability of your poor old mum and dad. And it's also about the untold, unacknowledged story of sadness that lay behind the angry blaze of punk and new wave. Watching this I thought of something I'd assumed lost for ever: my own feelings, aged 17, on hearing Buzzcocks' Sixteen: "… I wish I was 16 again / Then things would be such fun / All the things I'd do would be the same / But they're much more fun / Than when you're 21." Could it be, I thought, that I'm already sad about not being 16? 7 Miles Out is based on Morley's autobiographical novel of the same title , the once-upon-a-time-in-Stockport story of Ann, played with charm and zing by Lucy Halliday, and as a sweetly innocent young girl by Amelie Hughes. Young Ann pretends to be making a radio programme with her cassette recorder the way so many did in the 1970s, and hero-worships her would-be rock journalist elder brother Scott (Kasper Hilton-Hille) – based on Morley's brother Paul – who is already plugged into the burgeoning post-punk and new wave scene. Denzil Dias said, "We saw the film sometime in February this year and immediately felt that it had the potential to work in India. That tells you that audiences kept coming back, and more and more people discovered the film as the weeks progressed." Denzil then broke down the larger theatrical strategy behind films such as Obsession . With the phenomenal marketing teams at Warner Bros. and Universal, the focus then becomes ensuring that the supply is available – on the right screens, at the right showtimes and in the right markets." Denzil stressed that theatrical success today depends on much more than merely having a good film. How you deliver that story, how you market the film and how you nurture the audience are equally important." summary_long: Pitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & Me One man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It's an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of like Owen Wilson in Marley & Me , only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy. Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed. Continue reading...

Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane.

summary_long: Chris Fagan kept faith in his Lions which meant they could thrive with the weight of the football world upon them – and rip out Fremantle hearts There is no precedent for what happened at the MCG on Saturday. There have been devastating finals losses before – the Bulldogs losing the 1997 preliminary final to Adelaide and St Kilda losing the 2009 grand final to Geelong immediately spring to mind. A senior St Kilda staffer described the rooms after that game as resembling "a casualty ward following a mass disaster". Thankfully, we don't talk about sport like that any more. The modern athlete and the modern sporting club is better able to put their world into some sort of perspective. The prevailing mood in the rooms, in the stands and on the trains on Saturday was a mix of desolation and bewilderment. Part of it was Fremantle's history.

summary_long: This Luxembourg-made movie about a couple who venture east to save their son features some impressive film-making Stippled with first-world guilt about income inequality even between fellow EU member states, this Luxembourg-made horror sprinkles a bit of liberal fairy dust over what is otherwise a pretty straight-up, if twisty, horror setup: a grunting, inarticulate and physically disfigured big baddie stalks the normie protagonists who shouldn't have come round these impoverished parts. Think Grand Duchy Chainsaw Massacre, though admittedly without any chainsaws. There are sullen locals, a dilapidated farmhouse full of ominous clutter, ill intentions and horrible maiming. The unlucky visitors here are former couple Greg (Malik Zidi) and Anne (Brigitte Urhausen), who are co-parenting little Leo (Leo Todesco), a pre-adolescent who is lying in a hospital bed while waiting for a crucial organ transplant. A little time has to elapse before we learn that control-freak Anne blames likable doctor Greg for Leo's condition because he took his eyes off the kid for just long enough for him to get hit by a car. But Greg is trying to make it up to her by accompanying his ex on a trip to an unnamed eastern European country (where folks speak Bulgarian) to acquire the organ Leo needs on the black market, their glide path lubricated with lots of cash and pre-arranged bribes to border guards and the like. summary_long: Riverdale's Lili Reinhart does some heavy lifting in adaptation of Ali Hazelwood's hit book, but it's not quite enough Fans of the dearly departed Riverdale – or, moreover, admirers of all the batshit things the CW comic soap could make its bright young actors say with straining sincerity – have long rooted for Lili Reinhart. The Betty Cooper of yore was the best of that talented crop (Charles Melton and Camila Mendes among them) at rising above her subpar surroundings, her impressively expressive eyes able to sell the unsellable with complete conviction. She is the type of helplessly endearing performer suited to roles of naivety who masks surprise steeliness, as in her notable turn in 2019's Hustlers or, better yet, romcoms, though there remains a dearth of worthy material. (A dual role in 2022's Look Both Ways , a Netflix homage to Sliding Doors, didn't cut it.) At least on paper, The Love Hypothesis, a new romcom from Amazon Prime Video, should be that material. The BookTok sensation by neuroscientist turned author Ali Hazelwood presents an ideal Reinhart protagonist: extremely nerdy, in a periodic table way, yet conventionally beautiful, awkward and self-deprecating yet cutting when it counts, the type of sweet-presenting young woman who will shout "fuck" repeatedly in private. Which Reinhart's Olive Smith, a young biology PhD student at Stanford, winsomely does in the film's unsettlingly cold open, as a bleary-eyed Olive, blind from expired contacts, freaking out before her grad school interview and then boldly stating her cancer-solving intentions to a brusque, handsome professor in a lab bathroom. summary_long: Fast bowler won the Ashes and two World Cups but those successes were punctuated by long spells out with injury To reach for the career stats on Cricinfo is no way to go about it. This is a full-on YouTube job: boil the kettle, load up those spells at Headingley, St Lucia and the rest, and take in the whippy, absurd, mesmerising sight of perhaps the fastest English bowler there has ever been. That's probably the best way to remember Mark Wood's career. Tuesday's announcement of his international retirement was coming from the moment Wood hobbled out of the Ashes last December, the series opener his only appearance. That always felt like the last act, one he rushed back for after surgery on his left knee earlier that year, and the game moves on fast. England's seam stocks look healthy across formats, with Jofra Archer there to ramp it up when required. It's a sore point that Archer and Wood played just two Tests together: one without supporters during the 2020 Covid-bubble summer, the other Wood's farewell at Perth.

summary_long: One man's irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu's exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it's disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise's boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film's value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner. An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called "Digger" Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol'-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens's bomb-riding army major in Kubrick's Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.

summary_long: Veteran filmmaker Singeetham Srinivasa Rao is no more. The legendary director took his last breath at Kauvery Hospital in Chennai on Saturday, August 4, 2026. His last directorial was Sing Geetham , an experimental musical comedy film, which he helmed at the age of 94. Over a career of more than six decades, he worked in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam and Hindi cinema. Singeetam Srinivasa Rao has delivered several iconic films in Indian cinema that are often regarded as being ahead of their time, earning him the reputation of a visionary filmmaker. His works include several memorable titles, including the silent black comedy Pushpaka Vimana (1987), the time-travel film Aditya 369 (1991), the dance drama Mayuri (1985), and Kamal Haasan's Apoorva Sagodharargal (1989), Michael Madana Kama Rajan (1990), and others. Singeetham Srinivasa Rao was not only a director but also a screenwriter, producer, actor, and composer.

summary_long: Traditional woods have had a good innings but rising temperatures mean the need to find alternatives is pressing What happens if you run out of trees? It is a situation cricket must face in the perfect storm of an expanding game and more precarious growing conditions due to accelerated climate change. summary_long: Austin Abrams gets eaten by a sperm whale in an overlong and flashback-heavy adaptation of Daniel Kraus's hit novel that only has us on edge in moments Spare a thought for poor Austin Abrams, who, having just endured the world's worst, and gloopiest, courier assignment in Resident Evil , has now been trapped inside a sperm whale … The immensely likable Euphoria alum (has any show in recent memory provided quite as many genuine stars?) brings what he can to Brian Duffield's rather soggy adaptation of Pulitzer prize-winner Daniel Kraus's acclaimed novel Whalefall. But there's not a great deal he can do, despite being in every scene of what's his second studio lead in a month, other than scream and writhe and look understandably alarmed. It's a setup that's grabby enough to have us wonder just how the hell it's going to play out (what if that one scene in Finding Nemo but a whole movie) but it just doesn't work as a 106-minute adventure, too overstretched and too silly to have us rooting for his escape and caring how he might orchestrate it. summary_long: Singer Hayley Kiyoko misses the mark in a meandering directorial debut packed with groan-inducing dialogue On 26 June 2015, the US supreme court finally declared gay marriage legal nationwide. Two days later, singer-songwriter and former Disney Channel alum Hayley Kiyoko effectively came out to the world with her debut single, Girls Like Girls . "Girls like girls like boys do, nothing new," she sang with triumphant bluntness. Its accompanying music video, featuring a Sapphic teen romance, spread fast and wild across Tumblr, a website defined by its intensely nostalgic aesthetics, where style and identity formation merged for many queer teens. Today, the music video has 163m views on YouTube. Kiyoko, now engaged to former The Bachelor contestant Becca Tilley, has since been hailed the "lesbian Jesus" by fans. Queer expressions in pop music, from King Princess to Chappell Roan to Reneé Rapp , have become far more common in the decade since the music video was released, but Kiyoko still seems to inspire one of the most dedicated, and specifically Sapphic, audience in queer pop music today.

summary_long: A priest investigates his daughter's kidnapping in Thailand in this Paul Schrader-esque inquiry into spiritual nihilism 'He's American, a little bit overweight, sweaty, a little bit camp, creepy." As far as descriptions of border-hopping paedophiles go, this seems a little on the nose. So it's not surprising when the man who was enquiring, priest Father Daniel (Steve Oram), responds: "Are you making this up?" Featuring a seedy child-abduction situation in Bangkok, Simon Rumley's thriller comes close at times to bugged-out exploitation flick territory – but lets its fleet and fresh manner carry it towards a Paul Schrader-esque moral calvary. Pastor to a mixed Anglo-Thai congregation, Father Daniel has a young daughter, Olivia (Margaux Dietrich), with wife May (Nattapohn Rawddon). At a sleepover, Olivia is traumatised when her friend's older brother shows her a "crush" video of a kitten being stomped by a scantily clad floozy. So when her own cat Missy goes awol, she is convinced the same lady is responsible, and asks her dad how God could let it happen. The family mobilise to track down Missy, but Olivia in turn disappears one day after school, kicking off Father Daniel's own test of faith. Continue reading...

summary_long: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand? I must admit, I was apprehensive about meeting John Cena. The WWE wrestler turned actor has built an enviable Hollywood career playing idiots – capable idiots with real heart, but dimwits nevertheless. Still, Cena is obviously nobody's fool; fools don't rise from humble beginnings to become their generation's answer to Hulk Hogan or The Rock. Would the Cena who appears on my computer screen be the real one? Cena, 49, is speaking to me on behalf of Matchbox: The Movie, a film extension of the Mattel toy car brand for Apple TV, and for 45 minutes he is generous, funny, complimentary and elusive without ever being evasive.

summary_long: A childless woman flees into the forest and emerges with a swollen belly in director Didier Konings' short, sharp fable Before fertility tourism, the only option for your average medieval serf struggling to conceive was heading to the nearest foreboding woods and summoning weird, antlered dryads. Or so it seems from Didier Konings' short but memorable folk-horror debut, in which wide-eyed villager Frieda (Anneke Sluiters) flees into the trees after escaping an attempted rape by local butcher Gelo (Léon van Waas). He has already told her, after scoffing a pig foetus, that he likes his meat weak and defenceless. Previously chided for her lack of childbearing by husband Hikko (Len Leo Vincent), Frieda emerges with a swollen abdomen. But the villagers fear it is the devil's work, especially after finding Gelo in the woods, dismembered but freakishly still conscious. That's about the extent of the story here, but Konings pares the focus effectively down to the essentials of this obscurantist hole: the crawling fear of evil among the villagers, and the necessary projection of it on to everything outside their control – female bodies and emotions, the natural world. Though her character verges on symbolic, Frieda – as well as the "wise women" of the forest, as per the original Dutch title – allow this fable's feminist credentials to howl out unmistakably.

summary_long: Thrillers are built around tension. Whether they follow a detective chasing a killer or an ordinary person caught in an impossible situation, the genre is designed to keep audiences anticipating what might happen next. Thrillers can overlap with crime, horror, mystery, science fiction, drama, and even superhero movies, but suspense remains at their center (via FilmDaft ) . The best ones do not rely solely on shocking twists or constant action. They make uncertainty itself feel compelling, giving audiences a reason to keep watching even when very little is happening on screen.

summary_long: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan's blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year's other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it. After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: "That's exactly how I pictured it in my head." Or even less likely: "That was better than the book." We're more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year's Thursday Murder Club debacle. summary_long: England's identity under Steve Borthwick is not as clear as it should be this close to the tournament It was not so long ago that the Rugby Football Union would host an annual Christmas bash. Executives, head coaches, assistants, members of staff and an invitation to the press pack. Mince pies and mulled wine, even a touch of merriment if we were lucky. Eddie Jones would sometimes make an appearance, but the mind goes back to one year when he did not. To give him his due Steve Borthwick, his assistant at the time, did. He would probably rather have been anywhere else, but one of the more clear-eyed RFU employees, who had long-since figured out that the then forwards coach was destined for the top job, did their utmost to involve him. Alas, Borthwick soon had a long-distance train to catch and hours of in-depth analysis on a laptop ahead of him.

summary_long: Dave Franco and O'Shea Jackson Jr lead a goofy roadtrip comedy that is just sharp enough to keep you strapped in Idiots is billed as a return to the raunchy bro comedies of the 2000s like Pineapple Express and The Hangover and about halfway through there is a visual gag involving bodily functions that is so revolting, so unexpected and so genius that it comes close to them. For a moment, I was transported back to the mix of delight and disgust I felt upon watching a 90s Farrelly Brothers movie when I was far too young: How is this allowed? Described as an "earnest-dipshits-on-the-road screwball comedy" by director Macon Blair ( I Don't Feel at Home in This World Anymore , The Toxic Avenger), this R-rated indie comedy can't entirely deliver on that enticingly deranged promise, but it has enough testosterone-fueled transgression to make its runtime breeze by. Dave Franco plays Mark, a doofus with a neck tattoo who expresses affection for his fellow man by slapping them on the jowls. When he is invited to vacate his job at a call center – which he has been coasting through by playing gory video games and sneaking shots of whiskey at his desk – he teams up with Davis (O'Shea Jackson Jr) for a dodgy under-the-table job involving transporting wayward teens to rehab. Their first charge is Sheridan (Mason Thames), a moody influencer who has made a name for himself by playing cruel stunts on members of the public like an off-brand Jake Paul. Like Harold & Kumar before it, the road trip is an obvious but effective ruse for Idiots's freeform, THC-addled approach to storytelling which finds the trio jumping from country diner to crummy motel to a Slavic granny's living room as Sheridan attempts to derail his passage to rehab.

summary_long: Featuring: a teenager taking a debut hat-trick, a win for one of cricket's nice guys, and a hard summer for ground staff Tom Norton Not many people take a hat-trick on their Championship debut. Even fewer when they're a teenager. But in early May, 18-year-old Norton roared in like the north wind against Somerset and wrecked their top order. His delighted teammates chased him around Sophia Gardens, patting his impressive beard. By August, he'd been ruled out of the rest of the season with a stress fracture of the back. But, even without him, Glamorgan survived their first year back in the top tier, and batters will be nervously waiting in 2027. He made quite the first impression.

summary_long: India 211-6; Pakistan 192-6 in Twenty20 cricket final Captains refuse traditional pre-match handshakes India's men beat their fierce rivals Pakistan by 19 runs to complete a golden double in the Asian Games cricket after a pulsating final in front of a small but raucous crowd in Nagoya, Japan. The T20 world champions posted 211 for six in their 20 overs with Abhishek Sharma scoring 61 and Tilak Varma 51 not out, before Hasan Nawaz's valiant 96 saw Pakistan come up short at 192 for six. The neighbouring countries only meet in international tournaments and on neutral ground because of political tensions and the captains refused the normal handshakes before the match on Saturday. Afterwards, the jubilant India players paraded their national flag around the ground. summary_long: Boris Karloff's daughter and composer Michael Shapiro, whose musical score for the 1931 film is finally coming to London, talk about how it became a much-loved classic Once seen, never forgotten – the 1931 Frankenstein is 95 years old, but still one of the most instantly recognisable of classic horrors. Whether it's the sight of lanky Boris Karloff lumbering into the frame with his squared-off head, neck bolts and oversized leaden shoes, or the sound of a thunderclap and Colin Clive exclaiming "It's alive!" as the monster comes to life one stormy night in the laboratory – the film still raises hairs on the back of the neck. However, this classic has arguably long been missing one element: a continuous musical soundtrack – the original movie had dialogue but no music. In 2001, the American composer Michael Shapiro wrote a full-length score, which he will be conducting alongside the film for the first time in London next month, at Cadogan Hall with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. "It becomes one artistic expression, one artistic experience," he says. "The film and the music, together, and the audience forgets that I am there." Shapiro says his music emphasises what is already up on the screen. "Suddenly the film jumps out in a way it never did before." Continue reading...

summary_long: Sebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green light Blink a little and you might think we are back in 2019. The latest Spider-Man film, Brand New Day, has just passed $2.4bn at the global box office, to become the third-highest grossing film of all time behind Avatar and Avengers: Endgame. Meanwhile Avengers: Doomsday is reported to have already earned more than $50m in US ticket presales alone, despite the fact that it doesn't come out until December. Clearly we are in the middle of a superhero renaissance. And yet it doesn't really feel like it, largely because it is something of a turnaround for Marvel, after a pretty disappointing 2025 in which all three of the studio's releases underperformed. Captain America: Brave New World took $415m worldwide, Thunderbolts* managed $382m and even the well-reviewed The Fantastic Four: First Steps stalled at $521m, against a reported $200m budget.

summary_long: Thirty years after Diljale released, Harman Baweja has revisited memories from the film's sets, recalling an early experience that shaped his understanding of filmmaking. The actor, producer and writer was 15 when he visited the sets of the film, directed by his father and filmmaker Harry Baweja, and found himself trying to understand what exactly a director does while every department on a film set appeared to have a defined role. Harman remembers watching the shoot of 'Shaam Hai Dhuan Dhuan' , with Saroj Khan choreographing the song, Veeru Devgan handling the action and Naidu working on the camera. I was like, Veeruji is doing the action, Sarojji is doing the choreography, Naidu uncle is doing the camera work. Because everybody’s doing their job," Harman recalled. According to Harman, Harry Baweja's response became an early lesson in how different departments come together to serve a film's overall vision. summary_long: Adult performers on OnlyFans have taken to social media to question why Meta permits its AI agent Muse to engage in sexting while simultaneously restricting their own accounts. They argue that the AI’s permissive behavior creates a double standard that undermines their livelihoods. The creators point out that Muse can generate explicit content without the same scrutiny applied to human users. Meta’s decision has ignited a broader debate about AI ethics and the regulation of adult content online. In response, the performers are calling for a transparent policy review that treats AI and human creators alike. The controversy highlights the growing tension between emerging AI tools and the adult entertainment industry.
summary_short: OnlyFans creators are fuming as Meta rolls out its AI chatbot Muse, which can send explicit messages while the platform clamps down on performers’ own accounts. The disparity has sparked a backlash from adult entertainers demanding equal treatment.

summary_long: Amit Trivedi recently had a conversation with Komal Nahta, during which he spoke about the highs and lows of his career. He also made a touching revelation about the much-loved song 'Zinda' from Lootera (2013), starring Ranveer Singh and Sonakshi Sinha. The composer revealed that the poignant track was born out of a difficult phase in his personal life and was never originally intended for the film. When asked if there was any song in his discography that held a deeper meaning than listeners might realize, Amit Trivedi replied, "I composed a song called ' Mujhe Chod Do, Mere Haal Pe, Zinda Hoon Yaar, Kaafi Hain '. I wrote it for myself." When asked whether he had composed the song before beginning work on Lootera , Amit explained, "The film's work was going on at that time. It was not meant for Lootera but it became a part of it." At another point, he revealed, "I signed Shakun Batra's film, Ek Main Aur Ekk Tu , which was produced by Karan Johar. Aur mujhe kuch samaj mein nahin aa raha tha !" In many ways, Edward Scissorhands stands out as one of the best spiritual updates of Frankenstein ever made.

summary_long: For much of its history, the world chess championship was not a title a player could simply qualify to challenge for. From Steinitz–Zukertort in 1886 to the long disputes involving Lasker, Capablanca and Rubinstein, challengers had to raise money, negotiate terms and persuade champions to play. As Gukesh prepares to defend his title against Sindarov in Geneva, the USD 2.5 million match offers a striking contrast: the challenger has earned his shot through a formal qualifying system.

summary_long: It will be a tense time for Europe's longest serving president, despite the Champions League game at Anfield offering a symbol of how far they have come The first time Fernando Roig watched Villarreal play as their president, he sat in the stand at a tiny whitewashed ground that had concrete fever and was half empty. It was a Sunday night in the second division, they lost 3-0 against Badajoz, and he didn't enjoy it much. But then, he never enjoys it much. Even on Tuesday at Anfield, he will not: into his 30th year, the longest presidency in Europe, that is about the only thing that hasn't changed. More than 1,000 games and still it happens. "I don't get nervous," he says. I suffer a lot.

summary_long: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned David Kittredge gives us a thoroughly enjoyable, detailed account of the catastrophe that was John Boorman's 1977 film Exorcist II: The Heretic, the deeply ill-conceived and widely derided follow-up to The Exorcist, a bizarre but ambitious fantasy supernatural rhapsody, brimming with unintentional comedy. Yet it was visually bold and even brilliant, pioneering in its use of Steadicam; Linda Blair and Max von Sydow were persuaded to return; Richard Burton was cast as a troubled priest, and Louise Fletcher as a psychiatrist whose weird "mind-reader" contraption was entirely ridiculous. At the first film, people screamed. Now they screamed with laughter. According to an apocryphal tale gleefully repeated by William Friedkin, director of the first film, the sequel resulted in an enraged audience one night turning round and booing Warner Brothers executives in the back row of the cinema, and then chasing them out of the building and down the street. Boorman desperately recut the film with the sillier bits removed. But the damage was done.

summary_long: The Leeds player was surprise starter against Spain but, after his solid display, Jordan Pickford's grip may be loosening James Trafford looks genuinely affronted. Defiance is the stock in trade of a goalkeeper and Trafford has a nice line in it, on and off the pitch. Thrust into the England lineup against Spain at Wembley on Saturday for only his third cap, he performed well, particularly during the opening 35 minutes when the world champions threatened to run riot. Trafford made two excellent saves that kept England in contention, laying the groundwork for their surge into a 2-1 half-time lead. They ended up losing 3-2 in the Nations League opener after Harry Kane missed a 54th-minute penalty for 3-1.

summary_long: 2026 has quietly been a massive year for Tom Hardy , despite him only starring in one new project. The age-old saying goes something like "there's no such thing as bad publicity," and although Hardy came under the microscope earlier this year, it all worked out for the best. News broke back earlier in the summer that Hardy had been fired from his role as Harry Da Souza in MobLand , but considering he had already filmed all of his Season 2 scenes, this firing wouldn't take place until Season 3. This report has since been debunked and not only has Paramount confirmed that Hardy will return in Season 3 , the studio has even doubled down and renewed MobLand for Season 3 while Season 2 continues to dominate watchlists around the world.

summary_long: New York film festival: The follow-up to 2023's Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects Even by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago. Godzilla Minus One , the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in a series of Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn't just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and the Toho -made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience with Godzilla to overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to "zero", hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to "minus one". Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn't seen directly in trailers, this isn't a spoiler; he's featured from the very first scene of the film.) Continue reading...

summary_long: Bhumi Satish Pednekkar has raised her voice once again to extend an appeal to citizens to support those affected by floods in Bihar. The actress took to her social media handle to share a video, highlighting the gravity of the situation in Bihar and how her collaboration with Bharat Disaster Relief Foundation (BDRF) is extending aid on the ground. "Bihar mein picchle 45 dino se aise kayi ilaake hain jaha par abhi tak paani neeche nahi gaya hain. Unke paas koi zariya nahi hain ki wo apna khaan-peen, anaaj, kapde, auraton ke liye sanitation – bathroom nahi hain…itne saare parivaar aur itni saari communities hain jo relief camps aur tents mein reh rahi hain," she says. Bhumi highlighted that this time too, she has collaborated with the BDRF team to provide relief to flood-struck Bihar. "Iss waqt Bihar ko humari bahot zyada zaroorat hain," she says and urges citizens to unite once again to help those affected by the floods by extending support through any means possible. summary_long: Flat racing's youngest champion jockey in more than a century on his relentless – and rapid – journey to the top Billy Loughnane's mum wanted him to be a vet. "You'd have to ask her why," he says with a smile that is rarely more than a second or two away. "I'd say money and an easier lifestyle, but I always wanted to be a jockey and made it very clear that was what I wanted to be doing. My parents and family have all been very supportive since." It seems fair to say that Loughnane's career choice was the right one. At Ascot on Saturday, the 20-year-old will be officially installed as Flat racing's new champion jockey and the youngest in more than a century. Pat Eddery was 22 when he won his first title, Frankie Dettori was 23, while Lester Piggott – who rode his first winner at the age of 12 – was twice that age when he landed his first championship. summary_long: The recent Oscar nominee lends gravitas to a decent matinee movie on gold smuggling For Ethan Hawke, 2025 was quite the year, showing impressively jarring range as both a bitter gay lyricist in Blue Moon and a demonic child-killer in Black Phone 2, both out at the same time in cinemas, a uniquely terrifying double-bill for diehards. He also led critically adored new noir series The Lowdown, airing simultaneously, all serving as reminder of how he's one of the hardest-working established actors we have. Not many five-time Oscar nominees have made eight films in the last four years (while also directing two other films on the side). It doesn't all hit (Raymond and Ray, anyone?) but there's something unusually invigorating about someone with his level of fame still seeming so excited about the many different opportunities he can maximise (this is, after all, the guy who made millions from his crafty back-end deal for The Purge). He's on far safer ground, at least as an actor, in The Weight, a conventional adventure drama about gold smuggling in the early 1930s, but his increased versatility has earned him an increase in confidence and while the work here might err more on the physical, he easily anchors the film. summary_long: The latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey's manic 90s comedy To be completely honest, whenever anybody asks what my favorite movies are, my list has some typical standbys: Goodfellas and It's a Wonderful Life among them. The holiday classic National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation is another. But there's one feelgood fave on my list that always surprises people: Jim Carrey's 1997 blockbuster Liar Liar. The movie (for the lack of a better word) lies on the bedrock of a simple premise: a lawyer and doting father is physically unable to tell an untruth due to a birthday wish. In the hands of a less competent creative team and cast, Liar Liar would have been yet another forgettable piece of 90s comedy junk; destined for the bottom of a discount VHS bin, forgotten as the years trudged on. But largely thanks to an unbelievable performance courtesy of Carrey, who was working with a smart and peppy script, the film ascends into rarefied air. Continue reading...

summary_long: Ranabaali, starring Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna in the lead roles, recently arrived in theatres. Now, Rashmika has drawn a comparison between her husband’s performance in the film and Allu Arjun’s portrayal of Pushpa Raj in Pushpa 2: The Rule. Ranabaali: Rashmika Mandanna links Vijay Deverakonda’s performance to Allu Arjun’s Pushpa 2 Speaking at a press conference, Rashmika Mandanna opened up about Vijay Deverakonda’s transformation into his character in Ranabaali. She said, “When I was seeing Ranabaali be Ranabaali, there’s a full difference between Vijay and Ranabaali. Drawing a comparison with Allu Arjun’s performance in Pushpa 2: The Rule, the actress said, “Of course, there was a similar experience in Pushpa 2 when Bunny sir was doing that. The actors who perform know the feeling.” Concluding her remarks, Rashmika reflected on her experience working with Vijay in their previous films, Geetha Govindam and Dear Comrade. Apart from Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna, the film features The Mummy actor Arnold Vosloo in a key role.

summary_long: Over the course of its more than five-decade run, Charles M. Schulz's comic strip Peanuts underwent all sorts of radical changes before settling on the beloved gang that fans know so well. Schulz was never one to shy away from bold moves, such as casting aside characters who failed to stick with readers, quietly erasing them from the strips, or even killing them off, yet he also proved willing to rethink his approach to new additions, effectively redefining them entirely for the better.

summary_long: Back in 2019, M. Night Shyamalan brought an end to his trilogy of gritty superhero films with the release of Glass , uniting Bruce Willis ' David Dunn, aka The Overseer, James McAvoy 's Kevin Crumb, aka The Horde, and Samuel L. Jackson 's titular Elijah Price, aka Mr. Glass, for one final confrontation. After the comic-inspired, more nuanced highs of Unbreakable and the horror thrills of Split , the final result was a bit of a mixed bag in the eyes of critics. Some saw it as an underwhelming final chapter in one of the more unique attempts at a connected universe of superpowered beings that predates the MCU. However, Shyamalan ultimately accomplished what he set out to do from the get-go — tell an origin story.

Season 4 is no different. Once more, our favorite "rewardist" heads back out into the wild to find those who have suddenly gone missing and bring them home as best he can. summary_long: Among M. Night Shyamalan 's filmography, three films are often hailed as his best work — the unconventional superhero hit Unbreakable , the psychological thriller The Sixth Sense , and his alien invasion flick Signs . However, over time, more critics have started giving The Village its flowers. Released in 2004, the period thriller was initially maligned for its twist that so many viewers expected given the director's previous three features and saw as illogical. Retrospectives have now acknowledged what the big reveal had to say about post-9/11 America, the War on Terror, domineering leaders restricting access to information, and the urge by some to isolate themselves from the societal pains around them.

summary_long: The man behind The Last Emperor had the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss along with the soul of a cineaste To say that movie producer Jeremy Thomas was British cinema royalty did not quite do justice to his meritocratic, democratic instincts. A brilliant and inexhaustibly creative man, self-effacingly charming and quietly spoken in a world of loudmouths and show-offs, and hypervigilant for new talent, was more like a cross between an entrepreneur, an enigmatically clever and kindly Cambridge don and the movie world's favourite cool uncle, or maybe cool great-uncle. Respectively son and nephew of directors Ralph Thomas and Gerald Thomas (of Doctor in the House and Carry On fame), he was born into the industry and as an independent producer combined the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss with the soul of a cineaste, backing his own instincts and passions, befriending film-makers and doggedly pursuing projects over years. summary_long: The singer's hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old self A lot of Hayley Kiyoko's teenage summers were spent waiting, bored and pining, as she sat at the computer willing her crush to message her back on AOL instant messenger. Like Coley, the 17-year-old protagonist of Girls Like Girls, the film the pop star has co-written and directed, Kiyoko fell hard for a girl who "put me through my own heartbreak and haunted me for a long time", she says. Although the 35-year-old singer became known by fans as "lesbian Jesus" following the release of her breakthrough single Girls Like Girls in 2015 (the film is an extended version of the story first told in the song's music video), feeling comfortable in her sexuality didn't actually come until after its release. Her gay identity was, at the time, the topic she was "the most scared of writing about", and the song's confident refrain "Girls like girls like boys do, nothing new" came from wanting to "manifest feeling confident". This means that at some point in the hierarchy there is a level from which a team cannot be relegated. Rugby union in England is in the midst of a long, torturous attempt to join the grown-ups, which is not easy given the total dominance in the prevailing culture of football, but it has recently taken the most politically charged step away from the madhouse by closing its top tier. summary_long: Sacha Baron Cohen's new film risks being outdated in a more rancorous era. But could it restore the personality-driven genre to big screens or end it altogether? For a man whose campaign slogan was once "Keep it real", Ali G has his work cut out in the reality of 2026. The big dog of Da West Staines Massiv was the character with whom Sacha Baron Cohen carved out his own niche of gonzo-gotcha comedy in the late 1990s – and now he's back with new film, Ali G: Who Iz I? It's not just Baron Cohen's career as an undercover operative that's on the line. It's the future of character-led comedy as a going concern, now that he seems to be the last man standing in this once-noble tradition – in cinemas, at least. To be clear, character comedy isn't merely comedy with characters; it's comedy filtered through a central persona that overlaps with the comedian playing it and whose subversive sensibility colours the entire work.

summary_long: Aaron Sorkin's attempt to return to the success of The Social Network is a strangely dated and incomplete look at a world that needs a sharper eye In retrospect, David Fincher's 2010 film The Social Network was a landmark for a quiet, even counterintuitive reason. Before the film was released, some questioned whether Aaron Sorkin, a writer not exactly known for his mastery of, nevermind obsession with, the technical sphere, was the right man to tell the origin story of Facebook. And while Sorkin may well have converted Mark Zuckerberg into terms he could better understand – namely, a motormouthed wiseass who deep down wants to impress a smart, serious-minded girl – he and Fincher also made one of the first internet-centric movies to treat online life as a natural extension of IRL dynamics, rather than the otherworldly tech portal seen in so many 90s internet movies. Granted, that's the whole deal with Facebook: its viral spread of social networking, something so simple and addictive that aunts, grandpas and co-workers everywhere could understand it. Yet understanding its simultaneous extension and distortion of the real world wasn't a given; four years later, for example, 2014's Men, Women and Children was widely derided for taking an alarmist approach to the internet as a haven for adults seeking an affair, teenagers nursing porn addictions and fame-hungry strivers of all ages. The Social Network, on the other hand, is remarkably nonjudgmental about the basic mechanics of Facebook, rooting its nascent flaws in the human weaknesses that birthed it. In retrospect, the movie only feels outdated to the extent that it underestimates Zuckerberg's grasping for power and the potential for grim carelessness that his online kingdom was built on.

summary_long: Formula 1 raced on the streets of Baku, Azerbaijan, this past weekend. Although the race predates Liberty's acquisition of the sport by a few months , it's a rather good microcosm of the sport as it exists today. The track is a real challenge; it takes place on dusty city streets lined with concrete walls and through a medieval fortress gate, followed by a 1.4-mile (2.2 km) flat-out blast to the finish line, with gusts of wind from the Caspian Sea a block away. It's interesting to look at, with Baku's mix of modern and classical architecture sharing the stage with a massive hospitality and pit lane complex. And since it wouldn't be F1 without some controversy, this year the race was held a day earlier than normal after F1 switched up its schedule to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan's celebration of its recent war with Armenia—it's almost as if Bernie Ecclestone had never left. The proximity of the walls leaves very little margin for error at the speeds F1 cars go around Baku. In Baku he would have a much tougher task.

summary_long: When his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary project Ross McElwee is the film-maker who spun home movies into art, framing himself and his friends and his son Adrian. The director used to film Adrian for a few minutes each month. It feels crass to compliment McElwee on his latest documentary, Remake, because it isn't the picture he'd ever have chosen to make. It is instead a grief-struck tour-de-force: a magnificent film about film-making and its real-world repercussions. McElwee filmed Adrian because he loved him, but now fears he might have hurt him. "I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive," he says.

summary_long: Ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake—set to launch in 17 days—a community member built a detailed Zelda timeline to bring nostalgic players up to speed before the Door of Time reopens. The creator leaned on Nintendo’s own chronology from Hyrule Historia and the company’s chronicle page, treating them as the definitive source. The visual cleverly branches at the end of Ocarina of Time into three separate eras, reflecting whether Link wins or loses, with each era rendered as its own thread on a cloth‑like diagram. Those threads converge again much later in the timeline, tying into Breath of the Wild. The author notes that assistance from Claude helped shape the design, and acknowledges the challenge of fitting the project between a day job and everyday life. The post has earned 86 points and sparked 34 comments from the community. Overall, the timeline offers an engaging way to navigate the complex Legend of Zelda continuity before the highly anticipated remake drops.
summary_short: With the Ocarina of Time remake arriving in just 17 days, a fan‑crafted Zelda timeline visual helps newcomers catch up on the sprawling saga. Using Nintendo’s official Hyrule Historia as a guide, the chart splits after Ocarina into three eras and reunites later with Breath of the Wild.

summary_long: It has been suggested in the past that Christopher Nolan expects no friendly fire before and after the release of his movies. These details emerged when Nolan famously severed ties with Warner Bros. and signed a deal with Universal to release Oppenheimer . The partnership began with a bang, as Oppenheimer wildly exceeded box-office projections and earned the coveted Best Picture honor at the Oscars. It also won Nolan his first-ever Best Director Academy Award. Unsurprisingly, he stuck with Universal for the release of The Odyssey , which has emerged as his highest-grossing film, with nearly $1.8 billion worldwide. However, Universal released another summer tentpole directed by an A-lister just six weeks before The Odyssey . The movie in question didn't live up to expectations, and ultimately wasn't a factor when The Odyssey debuted in mid-July.

summary_long: The pair's first feature-length adventure stars Jemaine Clement and Olivia Tennet, has a dreamy soundtrack and beautiful stop-motion visuals – fantastic family fun Kiri is a lively yellow dinosaur, Lou is an amiable purple palorchecie (a fictional beast, vaguely resembling a palorchestes , which in turn vaguely resembles a giant tapir) – and if you've been watching their CBeebies show, which hails from New Zealand and consists of 5-minute episodes, you'll know they're the best of friends despite their ingrained temperamental differences. But how did they become friends in the first place? For the uninitiated, Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! functions as an introduction to the characters and their world, while for fans it's a delightful origin story. At only one hour long, the runtime is toddler-friendly – and to be honest, there are plenty of films marketed at adults that could learn a lesson from writer-director Harry Sinclair's economical storytelling. (Sinclair is also the writer of the TV series, alongside Buffy the Vampire Slayer writing alum Rebecca Kirshner.) With the voice acting talents of Olivia Tennet (Freda in Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers) and Jemaine Clement (Flight of the Conchords), plus dreamy songs from Don McGlashan (Blam Blam Blam, The Front Lawn), Kiri and Lou Go Raaa! would arguably work superbly as an audiobook or radio show – except the visuals are a treat too. summary_long: Fighters have always provided rich material for stories on stage and screen and the appeal to audiences has not wavered Three of my greatest joys in life are watching sport, going to the theatre and playing violin. So it felt almost embarrassing to discover a classic play that combined all three, yet I'd never heard of it before. To be fair, Golden Boy has not been performed in the UK in more than 40 years and its curious premise may be one of the reasons. Written in 1937, it's about a gifted young violinist in Depression-era America who also has a talent for boxing and is lured away from music by the pursuit of fame and money in the ring. In the current London production he is played by Josh O'Connor, who Knives Out fans have seen with his fists up as a boxer turned priest in Wake Up Dead Man . O'Connor is no less convincing on stage than on film, attacking a heavy bag with the kind of power that does indeed make you worry for his precious hands. Nor is that ab definition entirely the work of a makeup artist.

summary_long: Emily Brontë's classic is reimagined with extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork impalings but plays it straight Where pornography once trod, horror has now become the genre that infiltrates and apes all others. With a host of out-of-copyright cartoon characters recently grave-robbed for not-so-fresh IP, now classic literature is apparently fair game for a gruesome glow-up, in this case, Emily Brontë's regular GCSE-botherer. But Becca Hirani's laboured reworking makes the book's gothic subtext crashingly, jugular-spurtingly textual. As in the novel, wide-eyed Mr Lockwood (Ross Townsend-Green) pays a courtesy call to his brooding landlord Heathcliff (Sky Cheema) at Wuthering Heights. But this time, his sojourn is more like Jonathan Harker's at Dracula's castle; everywhere he turns, the shrouded phantom of Heathcliff's beloved Catherine Earnshaw (Elle O'Hara) is lurking, and she leaves an extra dollop of gore on the windowsill in her famous nocturnal apparition. The tetchy host doesn't do much to put Lockwood at ease – even before he's trapped in the house by a bubo-inflicting malady. Between the hallucinations, the surly servants, and the weird absence of Heathcliff's rumoured son Linton, he begins freaking out that it's a different kind of moors story he's stumbled into.

It's prompted questions around money, tax rates, geopolitics and respect Back in September 1925, Frederick Wilson, sports editor at the Globe, explained the fear among hockey fans that Canadian teams might not be able to compete for players against the new US teams like New York or Boston that were entering the pro league. At the time, Wilson reassured everyone that, no matter the big US cash, everyone on the ice would be Canadian anyway. It took a long time for the US to catch up to Canada in on-ice talent. But now that it has, should we expect Americans to want to play anywhere else than the US? For 100 years Canada has worried that the US would just buy all the best hockey players. But now it makes its own and, as the new NHL season gets underway on Tuesday night, they want to go home.

summary_long: The star of Heated Rivalry does his best in this in this human-trafficking yarn, which gets progressively ickier and more exploitative Sketchy in every sense of the word, this sci-fi thriller is set in the not-too-distant future in a dystopian concrete city (actually mostly Bucharest looking like itself), where life is cheap but screenwriting conceits are clearly expensive, given most of the main ones here appear to be borrowed from other movies. Brother-and-sister twins Baxter ( Connor Storrie , from Heated Rivalry ) and April (Lilly Krug) are struggling to get by and mooching around the fringes of the criminal world, doing jobs on a spectrum of legality, though nothing especially harmful to themselves or others. He does petty crimes and she makes wigs and sells downloads of her own uncannily clear dreams (a nod to neglected 90s classics Strange Days and Until the End of the World where dream tech played key roles). Unfortunately, Baxter and his screw-up associate Ronny (Tourialay Akbari) fall into debt to and afoul with local kingpin Klein (Serban Pavlu), whose persistent use of Yiddish phrases and general parsimoniousness sets up the characterisation just on the edge of antisemitism. When Baxter cleans out his and April's joint accounts and still comes up short, someone takes April and her archive of recorded dreams/memories. Suddenly, the action jumps ahead five years in the future and April is both still missing and yet, at a local brothel, all too ubiquitous where it seems she's been cloned to make numerous sex workers. Continue reading...

summary_long: Reports that Jon Watts could make a new trilogy about a clan who have already saved and destroyed the galaxy several times over leaves you wishing for a newer world The Skywalkers: who are they exactly? A family that has moulded the entire Star Wars galaxy in their image, to the extent that nobody can really imagine the long-running space opera without them. For nearly half a century they have blown up Death Stars, built Death Stars, destroyed Jedi orders, rebuilt Jedi orders, fallen to the dark side, risen from the dark side, died heroically, come back as ghosts. Star Wars has occasionally attempted to escape them. It has made films and TV shows about stolen Death Star plans, bounty hunters, smugglers and rebels from entirely different corners of the galaxy. Ryan Gosling will soon appear in a Star Wars movie that, as far as we know, has absolutely nothing to do with them. Deadline reports this week that Lucasfilm has hired Jon Watts to direct the first instalment of a new trilogy continuing the Skywalker saga, written by Simon Kinberg, with Daisy Ridley reportedly being eyed to return as Rey.

summary_long: Before Anthony Hopkins' Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann's pioneering Red Dragon adaptation Five years before The Silence of the Lambs, there was writer-director Michael Mann's pioneering Thomas Harris adaptation Manhunter, now on re-release in a director's "final cut" for its 40th anniversary. It was his version of Harris's 1981 novel Red Dragon, a movie which features Dr Hannibal Lecter (here spelt Lecktor) in a relatively minor part, and played in a much more coolly matter-of-fact and downbeat way by Brian Cox, who is first discovered in his cell lying down with his back to the camera. It has long been a haughty, hipster film-bro affectation to claim that Cox is better in the role than Anthony Hopkins. (Lecktor's early acoustic stuff was great, you see, before he went electric as Lecter.) I think that's a bit obtuse, for all that Cox is of course very good. Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs is the definitive version: face it. But I will concede that Cox is more interesting than Hopkins by the time the latter came to make the 2002 adaptation of Red Dragon, at which stage the franchise had become a bit tired. Manhunter itself is a very interesting and watchable movie, but feels a little unevolved compared to Jonathan Demme's masterly guignol spectacle, although Demme clearly inhaled Mann's excitement at jets, 'copters and military hardware deployed at speed to bring down just one man. summary_long: New York film festival: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti and Tatiana Maslany lead an excellent ensemble in this dramatization of a failed conference on climate change In late October 1980, days before the election of Ronald Reagan , Congress summoned 20 experts in various fields to a beachfront hotel in Florida. Their mandate was simple: figure out how to address the dire threat posed to the climate by fossil fuel emissions, then deliver their recommendations to Congress in the form of a statement. Every word said during four marathon sessions over the next 36 hours – every disagreement or digression, tirade or truce – was recorded by a stenographer for posterity into a single document, hundreds of pages long, that stands as an artifact from a time when expertise was trusted, before corporate greed and political expediency mired "debate" about rising levels of CO2 in the atmosphere in a haze of misinformation and inaction. The fact that this meeting took place at all – that experts in climate, energy, law, philosophy, politics and more agreed on the fundamental facts, yet struggled to reach consensus on what to do about them – is fascinating, if perhaps not the most natural fit for a movie. This was, after all, a conference room of specialists sharing evidence via overhead projector. Continue reading...

"People define success in different ways," he says, "but I'm the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland.

summary_long: The 1926 film of Goethe's tragic tale of a man who sells his soul to the devil remains a spectacular feat of German expressionism The centenary of FW Murnau's silent fantasy-melodrama from 1926 is the occasion to ponder this mysterious film, taken from Goethe's 19th-century depiction of the alchemist and natural philosopher who sells his soul to the devil but, in a very high-minded climax of German romanticism, is redeemed by love. (Not love of God precisely, but love of a good woman; the word "Liebe" finally appears at the centre of Murnau's radiating vision of concentric circles conjured by the heavens, which annul his debt to the Evil One.) It is therefore very different from Christopher Marlowe's scarier and more unforgiving account of Doctor Faustus. Murnau's Faust is (obviously) concerned with and animated by evil, and there are echoes of his Nosferatu , made four years previously. In this film, Faust, having struck his bargain on a provisional 24-hour basis with Mephisto, finds that he is scared of a crucifix, like a vampire. It is also very much a film of Weimar Germany with its mad energy and streaks of garish satire and black comedy; the book-burning scene in which Faust immolates all his necromancy volumes, along with the Bible, is one which resonated with later events. (Perhaps it indirectly inspired Klaus Mann's novel Mephisto, later to be filmed by István Szabó .) Continue reading...

summary_long: "Rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea," Lukas Vogel writes in a lengthy blog post explaining how exactly he managed to render Doom using an SQL database. OK, that's not entirely accurate. The SQLDoom project uses a small Python client to handle input and output, drive the game's timing, and display each frame to the screen. Behind that, a series of CedarDB tables tracks the game geometry and state, while about 1,300 lines of SQL queries spread across 89 common table expressions implement the game logic and generate 35 bitmap framebuffers per second. In this, SQLDoom is a major improvement over Vogel's previous DoomQL project , which last year set out to build "a multiplayer Doom-like shooter entirely in SQL." Unfortunately, that effort ended up with raycasting-based, grayscale ASCII graphics that were more akin to the simplistic 90-degree-angled maps of Wolfenstein 3D . The newer SQLDoom, on the other hand, generates full-color 640x480 frames that look like they could have come from the original Doom executable. Read full article Comments

summary_long: Grand Final: Warrington 10-23 Wakefield Trinity are champions for first time since 1968 Do not let anyone tell you fairytales do not exist. This is not just a maiden Super League title, or indeed a first major trophy for almost 60 years. This is the culmination of one of the most remarkable sporting stories of our time: from the unfashionable, second tier side nobody really spoke about to the champions of England. Matt Ellis promised things would change. When he took ownership of his beloved Wakefield Trinity in 2023, he inherited a club on its knees. Just relegated to the Championship, with a stadium that resembled a building site and a squad of players nobody wanted a piece of. But he insisted that within five years, Wakefield would win their first major trophy since 1968 with his investment.

summary_long: The Yash Chopra Foundation (YCF), the philanthropic arm of Yash Raj Films, has expanded its Scholarship Program this year, selecting 11 students, including the first-ever scholars pursuing Robotics and technology-led courses. The Foundation continues to take forward the vision of legendary filmmaker Yash Chopra by giving back to the industry that has given abundant love to YRF for over 50 years. Through the YCF Scholarship Program, the Foundation supports the children of registered Hindi film industry and FWICE union members in pursuing higher education, offering financial assistance of up to Rs. 5 lakhs per student. While the program has traditionally backed students in media, film and creative disciplines, this year it extends to a wider range of professional and technical courses, including Robotics & Artificial Intelligence, Engineering, IT, Management, Law and Medical studies. Among the technology-led picks, Nidhi Subhashchandra Yadav is pursuing a B.Sc. in Robotics and Artificial Intelligence Systems at Thakur College, while Aryan Singh is studying B.Tech in CSE (AI & ML) at Thakur Shyamnarayan College of Engineering. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Yash Chopra Foundation (@yashchoprafoundation) Speaking about the initiative, Akshaye Widhani, CEO, Yash Raj Films, shared, “The Hindi film industry has always been built on the contribution of people working across every level of the ecosystem, and the YCF Scholarship Program is our way of extending that support to the next generation of their families. summary_long: Sherman's March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art This new film from revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee is an extraordinary work, arguably his most audacious use yet of autobiographical material while at the same time being a coruscating self-criticism of that same technique. Think of it as an artistic ouroboros (a snake eating its own tail). Remake is all at once about creativity, shame, love and loss, revelling in the way film can capture a moment of truth and honesty, but tempered by the knowledge that once a subject knows they're being filmed everything becomes a kind of performance. It's a film that works on so many levels and at the same time is so simple and direct. On that very simplest level, Remake starts out as a documentation of how Hollywood got in touch with McElwee and told him they wanted to make a fictionalised remake of his best-known film, Sherman's March . Made in 1985 with a one-man crew (McElwee himself), Sherman's March recorded the McElwee's trip back to South Carolina where he grew up; there he films his family, old friends, and himself as he continually fails to establish romantic relationships with various women, all of it lavishly slathered with his own warm, softly southern-accented voiceover. summary_long: Neverwinter Nights, released by BioWare in 2002, rode the coattails of the studio’s legendary RPGs—Baldur’s Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect and Dragon Age—and earned strong sales and critical acclaim at launch. Yet, unlike its more celebrated siblings, it never cemented itself in the mainstream gamer consciousness. What sets it apart is its distinctive gameplay engine and robust modding tools, which have fostered a tight‑knit community of creators and players. Two decades later, that community remains unusually vibrant, with thousands of active fans still logging in for multiplayer sessions and custom campaigns. The game’s enduring appeal lies in its flexibility and the nostalgic pull of classic BioWare storytelling. In short, Neverwinter Nights may be a hidden gem, but its loyal fanbase proves it still matters.
summary_short: BioWare’s 2002 RPG Neverwinter Nights, the studio behind Baldur’s Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect and Dragon Age, still boasts a surprisingly active community more than twenty years after launch. Despite solid sales and critical praise, the game never achieved the iconic status of its siblings, but its unique design keeps players coming back.

summary_long: New York Film Festival: The Geese frontman mesmerizes in a concert film that is both swoony and austere One night last December, weary from a busy week and the impending doom of winter, I hurried into Carnegie Hall to witness Cameron Winter. The Geese frontman was marking the end of a breakout year with a series of rapturously received solo acoustic shows, drawing the penitent for whom the 23-year-old's primordial voice struck some kind of destabilizing natural frequency. I had bought the ticket months earlier, after being hypnotized by Winter's beguiling debut solo album, Heavy Metal, and sat transfixed in the rafters, far from the Brooklynite's lanky, stygian presence before a single piano. So far, in fact, that I assumed the maybe-camera that came on stage at one point was a bit, perhaps a jab at our incessant need to film things from a very deadpan celebrity whose only non-music interlude that evening was to wordlessly stand, stretch and mockingly fight with the stage door, as if trying to escape his own momentous show. I emerged from the event teary, charged by what felt like a communion across time, and confused by a friend's text: "can't wait for the cameron winter PTA doc". Continue reading...

Monday night's Asian Champions League Elite game between Al-Nassr and the Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana had ended with a 3-1 win for the Saudi club coached by Ange Postecoglou, with Ronaldo, supported by Sadio Mané, scoring, the smattering of star names indicative of the lure of the Saudi Pro League. A safety warning issued 15 minutes before kick-off came two days after 13 people died and more than 300 were wounded by Houthi strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid international airport. summary_long: Primetime and You Can See Everything are both clammy, audacious awards contenders that challenge our sense of reality. Ahead of the release of his drama starring Robert Pattinson as a TV vigilante, the 30-year-old director talks crime, punishment and South Park To direct one movie that is on everyone's lips in awards season is remarkable. That is the position in which the 30-year-old Florida-born film-maker Lance Oppenheim now finds himself. Next month brings the release of You Can See Everything, the three-hour documentary which he co-directed with faux-naif deadpan imp Nathan Fielder, in which they spend a month living with the disgraced health-tech mogul Elizabeth Holmes before she begins her 11-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy. The film, described by Oppenheim as "head-spinning" and so shrouded in secrecy that Variety magazine's list of Oscar predictions identifies one of its cast members only as "[Redacted]", is expected to become the first documentary nominated for best picture. When I meet Oppenheim in a London hotel, it is to discuss his other hot ticket, Primetime, for which Robert Pattinson is the one attracting Oscar buzz. The Batman actor gives a high-wire performance as Chris Hansen, the sensationalist US television vigilante renowned for ambushing paedophiles on To Catch a Predator, which was a disreputable and highly addictive segment of the current affairs show Dateline NBC between 2004 and 2007.

summary_long: Plex, the media‑server platform known for sharing personal movie libraries, has partnered with ticket‑seller Fandango to embed a ticket‑purchase option on its US title pages for films still playing in theaters. Starting today, Plex users can click a Fandango button to view showtimes and buy tickets, with the integration feeding attribution data through Kochava for studios and advertisers. Fandango reports it sells tickets for 31,000 movie‑theater screens across the United States. Plex says its streaming service generates more than 100 million streaming decisions each month, and the new feature will tap into users' ratings and cross‑platform viewing habits to gauge audience intent. The partnership aims to monetize Plex’s content‑discovery strengths while giving studios clearer insight into how marketing drives ticket sales.
summary_short: Plex is now letting US users buy theater tickets straight from its movie pages by teaming up with Fandango, turning its discovery engine into a ticket‑selling portal. The move adds a Fandango button on titles currently in cinemas, linking viewers to showtimes and purchase options.

summary_long: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger's Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans When Barbarian , Zach Cregger's debut film as a solo writer-director, came out in 2022, it was a big success, creating a buzz among horror connoisseurs, garnering good reviews, and grossing $46m. Then his second film, Weapons , came out in 2025 and did even better. Mounting industry buzz around the project crystallised into a fierce bidding war; Jordan Peele was reportedly desperate to produce and, incensed by his failure to secure the rights, allegedly fired his managers. The rumours went viral, resulting in a wave of incredible PR that saw the film wildly outperform box office expectations and win an Academy Award (for Amy Madigan 's blunt-fringed, bonsai-pruning best supporting actress turn as instantly classic villain Aunt Gladys). Even if Cregger had not had a box-office smash that crossed over into awards contention, there would still be an atmosphere of hushed expectation around his next move. Thus, with just two features, Cregger had established a reputation for totally terrifying, utterly unpredictable and – most importantly – genuinely original movies.
