summary_long: Refn's film eludes definition as it moves through time and space, from doomy reality to strange dream worlds populated by quasi-Lynchian characters The title's first word should probably be "His". Nicolas Winding Refn has returned to Cannes with a bizarre new fantasia moodscape, a midnight movie of fear and dreamy disquiet, meaning … what, exactly? The setting of the film – a twist on the 60s pulp shocker of the same title by Norman J Warren – morphs and shapeshifts from place to place, with the antilogical procedure of a dream, from a supposedly real outer world to the inner space of hallucination and memory. It starts in a giant, empty hotel (whose colossal Stygian corridors are not unlike those in Refn's Only God Forgives ) in the middle of a digitally rendered dystopian city, wreathed in the kind of mist that tends to conceal a serial killer, and people here are frightened of someone called the "Leather Man". We move to the fictional action of a movie the hotel's inhabitants are (possibly) planning to make, or perhaps to the world of their fears and imaginings, their ideas occasioned by this ostensible realist premise. This is a story populated by quasi-Lynchian characters and gargoyles with strange nicknames – the whole imagined landscape, lit by Refn's throbbingly neon purples, reds and blues, looks like a nightclub in hell. The pace is doomy, sepulchral and slow; like Refn's TV series Too Old to Die Young , it moves at the pace of a zombie which has been shot but still keeps on shuffling forward.

summary_long: Certain dates remain etched in collective memory, and 26/11 is one such date for India. summary_long: Nine years after its first attempt, Tesla is back at it with the Roadster, employing decades‑old stunt technology to make the show car perform aerial tricks. At the rear, four oversized exhaust‑style pipes don’t emit hydrocarbons but instead fire 100,000 psi jets of compressed nitrogen. While the spectacle dazzles, the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes remain vague on the legality of such a feature on public roads. The article leaves readers waiting for official clearance before the high‑octane stunt can hit the streets.

summary_long: A taut, charged procedural from Dominik Moll follows a conflicted officer investigating violence to a teenage protester Dominik Moll's Dossier 137 is a serious, focused, if slightly programmatic movie about police brutality in France; there are docu-dramatic storytelling reflexes and a determined procedural tread. The movie takes its cue from the horrifying real-life cases of gilets-jaunes protesters in France's 2018 demonstrations who suffered near fatal injuries due to the police's trigger-happy use of the LBD gun : the lanceur de balle de défense or "flash ball" gun which (deafeningly) fires vicious rubber bullets. Stéphanie, played by Léa Drucker, is a conscientious police officer in the IGPN, the Inspection Générale de la Police Nationale, effectively the Internal Affairs bureau, investigating horrific head injuries suffered by a teen protester, which could only be caused by the cops' flash-ball weapons. She is divorced from a cop, Jérémy (Stanislas Merhar) who along with his new girlfriend – also in the police – is gloweringly resentful of what he sees as her bureau's disloyal undermining of the police, and the way she is questioning the corners they (supposedly) have to cut to keep France safe, especially after the Bataclan attacks . summary_long: A musician becomes obsessed with the haunted seat, but the potentially hilarious premise sleepwalks its way to an unsatisfying conclusion The indie indulgences of US film-maker Amanda Kramer – which often contain big names making small appearances – are such a puzzle; sometimes they work, sometimes they don't. I enjoyed her weird reverie about an imaginary 80s TV special, called Give Me Pity! , but not so much the 1950s-camp daydream Please Baby Please , with Andrea Riseborough. Now she gives us a film with a toweringly strange and potentially hilarious premise, on which the result does not in any way deliver. Yet there are moments of interest in the dreamy Lynchian drift that causes Kramer's films to float away from the audience. The actors deliver halting dialogue as if in a hypnotic trance, paralysed by the film's heavy conceit: Juliette Lewis plays a depressed single woman who turns into a chair. The scene seems set for some entertaining hijinks with visual effects, in which Lewis and the chair merge. What in fact happens is that Lewis's own body is supposedly robbed of its animating identity or spirit, which migrates into the chair while she becomes catatonic, a body flopped down on the bed.

summary_long: The lore of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, once bought by Martin Shkreli, is explored in a rambling film produced by RZA For every reason except one, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, the seventh album by the Wu-Tang Clan , should've been a commercial hit. The 31-track double album, recorded in secret between 2007 and 2013, reunited all of the remaining members of the hallowed Staten Island rap crew and featured eye-catching collaborators from the standard (Redman, offshoot group Wu-Tang Killa Bees) to the unexpected (Cher, Game of Thrones actor Carice van Houten). The sound, at least according to those involved, harkened back to the glory days of the group's beginnings in the 90s. But for years, almost no one heard it. The group only issued a single copy of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin – on CD, ensconced within layers of filigreed silver – with the stipulation, in legalese, that it could not be used for any commercial purposes for 88 years. The decree, either a stunt or a bold artistic statement on streaming's devaluation of music, depending on your generosity and perhaps your net worth, succeeded in drumming up plenty of hype. And if you were anywhere around the blogosphere or cable news in 2015, you may recall that the beneficiary of that hype – the purchaser and thus single intended listener of this $2m musical treasure – was one Martin Shkreli , the "pharma bro" widely despised for gleefully hiking the costs of prescription drugs for profit.

summary_long: The spaces can stand both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League's hunt for justice At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating , while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission's report refers to payments "not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement". Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season's Europa League. It's possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat. The filmmaker said, “We wanted Mahaan as a theatrical release; we imagined the interval block of Dhruv's entry on big screens, and its response. But unfortunately it went to OTT.” The director added, “That's why I want to take Mahaan 2 in theatres; it's a big dream for me. I'm not worried, as right from the start it's a Netflix film.” More about Mahaan Mahaan, starring Chiyaan Vikram and Dhruv Vikram in the lead roles, was released directly on the OTT platform Prime Video on February 10, 2022. The film follows Gandhi Mahaan, a commerce teacher who leads a quiet, middle-class life with his Gandhian wife, Nachi, and their son, Dada.

summary_long: Manville's academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibe Part cold war thriller, part Kafkaesque reverie, this movie takes us back to the sinister drear of Poland in 1981, when General Jaruzelski has just introduced martial law in reaction to the dangerous new mood of freedom occasioned by the Solidarity trade unions. The director is Kasia Adamik, daughter of The Green Border's Agnieszka Holland; the film is adapted from a story by Olga Tokarczuk, called Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw. Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, an academic clinical psychologist (like Tokarczuk) from Britain with testy, peremptory mannerisms; her indulgence is a fondness for taking Polaroid photos. She has attained a certain level of celebrity for a book on dreams, despite claiming that she never dreams herself. Andrews has been invited to give a lecture in Warsaw, during which she begins to outline views on mental illness not unlike those of Laing or Foucault; but her speech is chaotically disrupted by students shouting that Poland itself is an oppressive asylum. Continue reading...

summary_long: Three holdover hits — Resident Evil , Heart of the Beast , and Primetime — managed to outperform the divisive new movie starring Tom Cruise , Digger . Directed by two-time Oscar winner Alejandro G. Iñárritu , the satirical epic is shaping up to be a historic bomb, and the circumstances surrounding its release seem appropriately dour. Digger is the final movie in Warner Bros.' century-long run as an independent entity, and the last to be released under the leadership of the dismissed studio chiefs Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca . Produced on a budget that has been reported to be anywhere between $140 million and $180 million, the movie was projected as an Oscar play for Cruise, but its mixed critical reception and disastrous box-office results may dent his chances.

summary_long: The Drishyam franchise has come a long way at the box office, and the opening-day numbers of its three films tell that story rather clearly. Drishyam The Conclusion , the latest and final chapter of the Ajay Devgn-led franchise, has opened with a massive Rs. 62.03 crore at the India box office. To put that number into perspective, the original Drishyam had opened at just Rs. 5.80 crore when it released in 2015. Its Rs. 62.03 crore opening is more than four times the opening of Drishyam 2, representing an increase of Rs. 46.65 crore. There is also a clear progression in the three opening days: Rs. 5.80 crore for Drishyam, Rs. 15.38 crore for Drishyam 2 and Rs. 62.03 crore for Drishyam The Conclusion. With its latest chapter, the franchise has therefore gone from a modest Rs. 5.80 crore opening in 2015 to a blockbuster-level Rs. 62.03 crore start in 2026, marking a remarkable evolution for the Drishyam series at the box office. summary_long: Game of Thrones fans have been delighted by the spin-off shows House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms. Now, the makers are all set to introduce the first-ever film in the universe, exploring the story of Aegon Targaryen’s conquest. Game of Thrones: Aegon’s Conquest - Everything to know about the film The world of Game of Thrones is heading to the big screen for the first time. Warner Bros. has announced a theatrical release date for Game of Thrones: Aegon’s Conquest, a new film set centuries before the events of the original HBO series. The movie will explore one of the most important chapters in Westerosi history, particularly Aegon Targaryen’s conquest of the Seven Kingdoms. Unlike House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, which are television spin-offs, Aegon’s Conquest is being developed as a theatrical feature. The conquest took place roughly 300 years before the events of the original Game of Thrones and about a century before House of the Dragon .

It got even worse for Pierre Sage after Brighton extended their lead through Gómez's wonderstrike and Yasin Ayari, with Charalampos Kostoulas adding a fourth after half-time and the substitute Jack Hinshelwood's late strike matching their record 5-0 win over Palace from 1956 in Division Three South. summary_long: Alex Gibney’s documentary about Elon Musk is set for a broader release, but TikTok announced a permanent suspension of the film’s social‑media account ahead of that rollout. The ban was first reported by The Hollywood Reporter and later echoed by The Verge, with TikTok declining to comment when asked. Bleecker Street, the film’s distributor, was informed of the impending suspension on a Friday afternoon and has yet to issue a statement. Although TikTok has no formal ties to Musk, the documentary features a cameo by Oracle co‑founder Larry Ellison, who appears via a text message offering to help fund Musk’s Twitter purchase. The film also includes footage of Musk at the Capitol One Arena inaugural parade in Washington, D.C., captured by AFP. The sudden account removal adds to recent scrutiny of major platforms—including YouTube, Meta, and X—over their handling of high‑profile tech documentaries.
summary_short: TikTok has permanently suspended the official account for Alex Gibney’s upcoming Musk documentary, just as the film nears its wider release. The move was reported by The Hollywood Reporter and confirmed to The Verge, leaving distributor Bleecker Street scrambling for a response.

summary_long: While Netflix enjoys the success of East of Eden , Prime Video is prepping for the release of an entirely different (but just as influential) literary adaptation. This week, the streamer will debut a new and updated limited series based on Stephen King 's first-ever novel. The book has famously been adapted previously into a 1976 movie directed by Brian De Palma , and then a remake directed by Kimberly Peirce and released in 2013. The new version counts King himself as an executive producer, with his longtime collaborator, the legendary Mike Flanagan , serving as creator. Flanagan previously directed the King adaptations Gerald's Game , Doctor Sleep , and The Life of Chuck .

summary_long: It was a risk for Star Wars: The Clone Wars' three-season sequel to move away from the Jedi, but it paid off. Star Wars: The Clone Wars is one of the most important stories in Star Wars canon. Set between Star Wars: Episode II — Attack of the Clones and Star Wars: Episode III — Revenge of the Sith , it provided invaluable context around the Jedi Order's downfall, the Separatists' politics, Palpatine's orchestrated rise to power, and Order 66 . It fixed and addressed many of the prequel trilogy's biggest issues and mistakes, including Darth Maul's untimely death and Anakin's relationship with Padmé Amidala.

summary_long: The impact of colonial then corporate agricultural development is unravelled in a sobering documentary that takes a dramatic turn when a family secret is discovered The central highlands of Kenya are renowned for their lush tea plantations, which stretch as far as the eye can see. Most of the field workers come from the Kikuyu community, whose farming traditions span centuries. In Andrew Harrison Brown and Bea Wangondu's sobering documentary, these resplendent vistas are also enshrouded in misery. Opening with a televised speech by Evelyn Baring, the colonial governor of Kenya during the 1950s , the film lays out the imperialist impetus behind Britain's agricultural development of the country. The Kikuyu people were stripped of their ancestral lands, their labour extracted to enrich their colonisers. This system of inequality continues until now, with multinational corporations taking up the playbook of exploitation left by colonial control. There's the decades-long struggle for justice undertaken by Mr Mungai, a pastor and activist who has fought numerous court cases to reclaim his family land.

summary_long: Led by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom's directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrong Time loops often feel like the movies' favorite zany stylistic trick: Bill Murray plotting to win Andie MacDowell's heart, a college student solving the mystery of her own grizzly murder, or as a ruse for Anne Hathaway to face off with a T rex . The excellent new indie horror film It Ends takes a different approach with its nightmarish depiction of a carful of friends stuck in an endlessly repeating day. It's less of the moony japes of Groundhog Day or Palm Springs than an arthouse spin on the Prometheus myth, with the unfortunate souls of the film cursed not with death but with the torture of eternal life. After helping their friend move into a new apartment, a crew of aimless twentysomethings take a late-night drive to get food, but after GPS leads them deeper and deeper into a desolate forest, it's clear that they have lost their way. When they pull over, they are set upon by a group of people that look eerily similar to them – young people who are dressed like they stepped out to the corner store and couldn't find their way back. "They look scared," one character says with a pained expression. "Why are they scared?" Continue reading...

summary_long: Alex Gibney's documentary follows the celebrated author's life up to and after the attack, but what shines through is Rushdie's remarkable courage The terrifying, inspiring story of how Salman Rushdie survived and thrived after the assassination attempt on him in New York in 2022 is the subject of this excellent documentary from Alex Gibney. It is based on Rushdie's own memoir , narrated extensively by the author himself, and using the intimate hospital-bedside video footage shot by his wife, the poet Rachel Eliza Griffiths. There are stomach-turningly explicit shots of Rushdie's damaged eye and also, finally, horrendous scenes of the attack itself. What emerges is Rushdie's courage and his remarkably level-headed, calm and unafraid writerly voice insisting on the primacy of literature, freedom of expression and the life of the imagination. The film itself takes us from Rushdie's childhood in Mumbai (with a certain unselfconscious locution of his class and background, Rushdie still calls it "Bombay"), to the years of bullying and unhappiness at an English public school, then Cambridge, London, his day job in advertising (he is cheerfully delighted by his successful campaign for Aero chocolate). Then there is writing fiction and the big breakthrough with his magic-realist creation myth Midnight's Children. We get a lot of footage of him in black-tie at awards, which is how he appeared in the media: a crude jihadi placard actually shows him in a bow tie.

summary_long: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey might be the one to beat but a crop of competitors is starting to materialise Reporting from fall film festivals used to be a more streamlined process – what's good, what's bad, what's being sold, what has Oscars chances – but with each year, the season arrives with larger, more existential questions. The 2025 run, from Venice to Telluride to Toronto, was notably underwhelming and took place months after Sinners went from box-office hit to legitimate contender and at the same time as One Battle After Another skipped festivals and went on to win best picture . The pipeline that had once birthed winners such as Birdman, Spotlight, 12 Years a Slave and The King's Speech had no longer played as big of a part with Covid-affected Nomadland being the last fall festival film to win the top prize. Even without an awards hat on, there has been a more general lack of buzz, an excitement of something new that much harder to find as more films of considerably lower quality took up underserved space. If the trades are to be believed, a lot of it is down to studios choosing against the risk of bad buzz and potential embarrassment to A-listers because for every The Shape of Water or Poor Things, there's a White Noise or Joker: Folie à Deux. So while this season might see new films starring Tom Cruise, Timothée Chalamet, Anne Hathaway, Christian Bale, Amy Adams, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Ben Affleck and Mikey Madison, none of them are braving a festival premiere. Continue reading...

summary_long: This over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life Frantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation. You could make the same argument against plenty of live-action films of course, but it is in animation that this kind of soulless blitzkrieg tends to predominate. Forgotten Island is over-controlled and over-determined, a movie that never, or hardly ever, takes its pedal from the metal, never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. At times it seems to be aping the world of Japanese anime, but without its sense of character or capacity for calm. The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in the Philippines in the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline.

summary_long: Spanish drama about people leaving their old lives behind plays out like a literary novel, with Manolo Solo excellent as a discombobulated gardener Out of the blue, a woman walks out on her husband. Bags packed and ready to go, at the last moment she crumples up the letter she has written to him and vanishes from their Madrid flat. So begins this drama featuring not one but three characters disappearing without a trace from their lives; it sounds soap opera-ish, but mostly The Portuguese House unfolds as polite elegant drama, told with such rich novelistic detail it often feels like it's getting into the minds of the characters. Manolo Solo gives an excellent performance as the left-behind husband, Fernando, an introspective mild-mannered geography professor. After his wife's disappearance, Fernando goes on holiday to Portugal, where he meets a gardener called Manuel. When Manuel drops dead of a heart attack, Fernando decides – like his wife – to leave his old life behind; he assumes Manuel's identity and takes a job as the gardener at a Portuguese country estate. The owner, Amália (Maria de Medeiros), senses that this intellectual man with glasses and a clumsy way with the loppers is not the man she hired, but doesn't push it – possibly because she is attracted to him.

So begins this drama featuring not one but three characters disappearing without a trace from their lives; it sounds soap opera-ish, but mostly The Portuguese House unfolds as polite elegant drama, told with such rich novelistic detail it often feels like it's getting into the minds of the characters. summary_long: Academy Award winner Jessica Chastain is all set to be seen on the big screens in the horror film Other Mommy . The Rob Savage directorial appears to lean heavily into psychological tension, uncertainty and paranoia. With Bela unable to determine who is trustworthy and whether what she sees is real, the film aims to keep viewers questioning every character and moment. Rob Savage reveals there are ‘50’ jump scares Speaking to Entertainment Weekly about the film’s scares, Savage was asked how many jump scares audiences can expect. I think crafting a really great jump scare can sometimes happen without the classic ‘quiet…quiet…loud’ formula that everyone associates with jump scares.” He further adds, “The film plays the hits of every aspect of horror. It’s full of dread, it’s full of set pieces, but it’s all steeped in this deep paranoia where you’re wondering if what you’re seeing is reality, if who you’re seeing is Ursula or Other Mommy, if you can trust any of the grown-up characters.” About Other Mommy Based on Josh Malerman’s bestselling novel, the film follows Bela, a young girl who encounters a mysterious entity inside her home that looks eerily identical to her mother. Apart from Jessica Chastain , Arabella Olivia Clark plays Bela, with Jay Duplass portraying her father, Daddo.

summary_long: Race to be named the world's best female player is the most open in years. But who should claim the prize? 1 Melchie Dumornay (OL Lyonnes/Haiti) Yes, Dumornay was part of a team that lost 4-0 to Barcelona in last season's Champions League final , but her influence in the OL Lyonnes midfield as they cruised to a domestic treble stepped up a gear. The technically brilliant 23-year-old midfielder was named player of the year by the French players' union, and her importance to Lyonnes was most clearly demonstrated by her absence through injury for their 2-1 loss to Arsenal in their Champions League semi-final first leg. She returned for the second leg and produced a player-of-the-match performance in a 3-1 win . Dumornay scored five goals in Lyonnes' Champions League run and was named in the team of the tournament. 2 Ewa Pajor (Barcelona/Poland) After losing five Champions League finals, Pajor shook off her 'always the bridesmaid, never the bride' mantle in style with two goals as Barcelona thrashed Lyonnes in Oslo. The 29-year-old's 11 goals in European competition last season matched Alexia Putella's 2021-22 tally, which has not been bettered since Ada Hegerberg's record-breaking 15 in 2017-18. Pajor also scored 16 goals in Liga F, behind only her Barcelona teammate Claudia Pina who scored 21.

summary_long: The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He's hoping his new venture can recapture some headway When Maga media blowhard Clay Travis offered $2m to Colin Kaepernick last week to appear on the daily talkshow he hosts with former CIA analyst Buck Sexton, it represented the culmination of a years-long obsession on the right with the onetime NFL star. In Travis's telling of history, Kaepernick taking a knee during the 2016 NFL season was the event that catalyzed professional sports into the era of "woke" excess from which, he claims, it has been struggling to recover ever since. But more than simply confirming the right's longstanding villainization of Kaepernick, Travis's offer was also a smarmy bid for publicity for his new media venture, Sport & State. Sport & State, which launched in August, is Travis's bid to get back to his roots as a media mogul who sold the wildly popular Outkick to Fox Sports for a rumored $100m, and reclaim some of the cultural territory lost to fellow sports bros and Magagitators like Pat McAfee, Joe Rogan, Tucker Carlson and Ben Shapiro. But if there's one thing Sport & State won't be doing, it's engaging with anyone beyond the Magaverse. No one associated with the left or progressive politics ever appears on Travis's shows, for the simple reason that they are designed purely for the right to talk to itself. (Some would say the same could be said of the left, although the disregard for dissenting perspectives in the Magasphere seems way more extreme.) More than it heralds a renewal of Travis's career or an injection of fresh energy into the Trumpist mediasphere, Sport & State is a case study in the stagnation that has taken hold on the right as Donald Trump stares down the barrel of defeat in November's midterm elections.

summary_long: Film producer is certainly not a typical owner of the second favourite for the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe with Maltese Cross part of a remarkable script As George Waud is the first to concede, he is not a typical owner of the second favourite for the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe. "No," he said this week, three days out from the most prestigious and valuable race of the European season, when his colt Maltese Cross will take on runners from racing's superpowers. "And for that reason, I'm making the most of it." The backstory that has led Waud to the Bois de Boulogne on the first Sunday in October started in London, includes 23 years in Los Angeles as he worked his way up from the bottom rung of the movie industry, and more recently, a co-producer role on the award-winning revival of Cabaret in London's West End. summary_long: Under the cover of night, anonymous personnel discuss AI, error rates and problematic intelligence units in a documentary produced by the Guardian Here is a disquieting documentary about what Israel's military chiefs in Gaza reputedly call "Naza", meaning civilian collateral damage – itself a queasy euphemism. The calculated "Naza" number is the amount of projected civilian deaths from each military strike, and perhaps it will come to have the same connotations as the US military term "body count" during Vietnam. The directors are Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the film-makers behind No Other Land , which was about attacks by the Israel Defense Forces on Palestinian West Bank villages. NAZA is executive produced by Jonathan Glazer and James Wilson and appears under the production auspices of the Guardian, in which some of the stories have already appeared. There are flaws: interviews were conducted on the condition of anonymity, but if no-one can be persuaded to put their name and face to their words (and of course it is terribly dangerous) then the impact of this as testimony is lessened. But even so, the film is casting a chilling light on what is happening now in Gaza. Continue reading...

summary_long: “You Can See Everything,” the latest documentary from comedian‑director Nathan Fielder, dives into the world of former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes. By placing Holmes alongside Fielder’s dead‑pan humor, the film creates a constellation of colliding personas that constantly question what is real. It treats the high‑profile tech scandal as both a true‑crime case and a satirical study, blurring the lines between documentary and performance. Throughout, Fielder’s trademark awkwardness amplifies the tension, making every interview feel like a staged experiment. The result is a thought‑provoking look at authenticity in an age of manufactured narratives, offering viewers a fresh take on a story that has already captivated the public.
summary_short: Nathan Fielder’s new documentary “You Can See Everything” pits the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes against his own off‑beat comedic lens, turning authenticity into a battlefield. summary_long: Drishyam 3 went on sale yesterday, and the response has been fantastic. The film is coming in with high expectations at the box office, given the strong IP value and its release on a major national holiday. At the time of writing, the film has sold around 35,000 tickets across the two national chains. The advance is currently coming only from multiplexes, with the smaller chains like Miraj, Moviemax, Wave and City Pride also amassing a good advance. By the end of the day, the national chains figure should rise to around 45,000 tickets. That compares well with Stree 2, which had sold a similar number of tickets at the same stage before release. Stree 2 opened on Independence Day in 2024 and netted Rs. 50 crore on its opening day, which is the benchmark Drishyam 3 will be targeting.

summary_long: Nearly 25 years after its release in theaters, My Big Fat Greek Wedding has stood the test of time as a cultural touchstone of a rom-com celebrating Greek heritage and the many loving relationship dynamics within a family. Nia Vardalos wrote the film with heavy inspiration from her family life, giving each character and their little eccentricities a loose but very personal connection to reality that, in the eyes of critics and audiences, made them all the more human. The result was a relatable clash of cultures and search for identity as Toula Portokalos falls for a non-Greek man, played by John Corbett , and her loved ones continue to insert themselves into the wedding plans. Yet, one of the things best remembered about the feature, above its central romance, is its connection to Windex.

summary_long: The sports-mad city has embraced its new superstar, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philly was never his first choice Philadelphia has always had an instinctive affinity with athletes who embrace the grind over the glamour. In a place where sports mean a little too much, commitment has traditionally counted for more than celebrity. What it demands above all, sometimes unreasonably, is the sense that they have bought in, that the city and its fortunes matter to them as much as they do to the people who devote their lives to backing its teams. Few embodied that ethic more completely than Lane Johnson, the Eagles' revered right tackle and best player for more than a decade, who abruptly announced his retirement Tuesday after 14 seasons, two Super Bowl titles and a career spent neutralizing some of the most freakish physical specimens to walk the earth. Johnson's quotidian greatness on the offensive line was almost perversely workmanlike. According to Pro Football Focus, he allowed just 10 sacks across close to 7,000 pass-blocking snaps in the last 13 years, going entire seasons without letting his man bring down the quarterback. The Eagles won nearly two-thirds of their games when he played and lost nearly two-thirds when he didn't.

summary_long: He cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Exactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock'n'roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth's Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian's Michael Billington likened him to "an embryonic Elvis". Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violent DC Comics supervillain blockbuster set in Batman's stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther.

summary_long: J.R.R. Tolkien is one of the most revered fantasy authors ever. Among his several inventions were orcs, uruks, Balrogs, dwarfs, dragons, the Elvish languages known as Quenya and Sindarin , and the elves who spoke them. Legolas is almost certainly every Tolkien fan's favorite elf and for many reasons. Setting aside his good looks, Legolas was equally quite an agile figure, a competent warrior and brilliant archer, who never missed his target nor did his quiver ever run dry. A Sindar elf, Legolas was portrayed by Orlando Bloom in the critically acclaimed The Lord of the Rings trilogy directed by Peter Jackson .

summary_long: Through intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figure A titan of silent cinema, Austrian director GW Pabst left behind a treasure trove of classics. Working in Weimar Germany, Pabst gave Greta Garbo her second ever lead role in The Joyless Street (1925), and propelled Louise Brooks to international stardom with Pandora's Box (1929) and Diary of a Lost Girl (1929). Attentive to the marginalised elements of society, these early triumphs exemplified the kind of free-spirited film-making that flourished before the rise of the Nazi regime. Faced with this colossal legacy, Angela Christlieb's probing documentary takes a more winding path through Pabst's personal archive. Through intimate letters, family albums, and interviews with his descendants, the film foregrounds the man behind the images, while bringing another figure into the spotlight: Gertrude Pabst, the director's wife of more than 40 years. Far from a hagiographic portrait, Christlieb's film reveals Pabst to be a complicated and patriarchal figure. Pabst's films have been praised for their modern and strong-willed female characters, yet in private he forbade Gertrude from pursuing her own acting aspirations.

Around the same time, Christopher Nolan delivered his biggest-ever hit, The Odyssey , which outgrossed previous films such as The Dark Knight and Oppenheimer . Remarkably, The Odyssey has almost doubled the global haul of Inception . The movie still hasn't landed on the PVOD market, given Nolan's strict theatrical exclusivity demands, but audiences can revisit one of his past hits this October on Netflix.

summary_long: Bigg Boss Malayalam Season 8, hosted by Mohanlal , premiered on TV and OTT earlier, bringing intense drama at various moments. Now, contestant and actress Mridhula Vijai has opened up about her personal struggles, breaking her silence on them for the first time. Bigg Boss Malayalam 8: Midhula Vijai opens up about her personal struggles Speaking on Bigg Boss Malayalam Season 8 , Mridhula Vijai opened up about her childhood, the struggles her family went through, and the responsibilities she had to take on from a fairly young age. Talking about what home really means to her, Mridhula said, “If somebody asks which is your favourite place, I say the place where my favourite people are, that is my favourite place. For now, my favourite place is my house, which I built myself at the age of 25. From a young age, I lived in rented houses. I have lived in 13 rented houses.” Continuing, Mridhula mentioned that during her Plus Two years, her parents were involved in an accident, and nothing was quite the same after that.

summary_long: Super Scam Me, the latest National Geographic documentary, drops this Saturday at 9 p.m. ET and will later be available on Disney+ and Hulu. Host Mariana van Zeller dives into the dark world of romance scams, following a fake Instagram DM that pretended to be rock legend Jon Bon Jovi. Partnering with ethical hacker Arman the Cyber, van Zeller stages a sting using a counterfeit bitcoin receipt to bait the scammer and give a victim closure. The film blends investigative journalism with tech‑savvy tactics to show how easily love‑bombing can turn into fraud. The Federal Trade Commission reports that romance scams cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion each year, underscoring the documentary’s timely relevance. Viewers can expect an empathetic yet gritty look at how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” blurs in the digital age.
summary_short: National Geographic’s new documentary Super Scam Me premieres Saturday at 9 p.m. ET, then streams on Disney+ and Hulu. Investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller teams with ethical hacker Arman the Cyber to expose a romance‑scam impersonating Jon Bon Jovi, offering victims a chance at closure.

summary_long: Abhishek Bachchan has expressed his interest in returning to one of his most remembered songs, ' Kajra Re ', nearly two decades after its release. The actor recently recalled the experience of shooting the song from Bunty Aur Babli and said he would "love" to be part of a 2.0 version, although he jokingly noted that Aishwarya Rai Bachchan and his father, Amitabh Bachchan, would also need to be convinced. In a conversation with BBC Asian Network, Abhishek was asked whether he would be interested in revisiting ' Kajra Re ' with a new version. I’d love it. You have got to convince Aishwarya and my dad, though." Reflecting on the original song, Abhishek recalled the shoot as one of the most enjoyable experiences of his career. Released in 2005, Bunty Aur Babli featured Abhishek as a con artist alongside Rani Mukerji, while Amitabh Bachchan played the police officer pursuing them. ' Kajra Re ' featured Abhishek, Aishwarya and Amitabh together and became one of the film’s most remembered songs. summary_long: Marcus Smith's return from injury offers hope but Quins appear a fragile side beset by entrenched problems Speak to anyone who holds Harlequins close to their heart and a word that often comes up is "fragility". Fragile in defence against Gloucester last weekend but mentally fragile too. The scars of recent seasons are deep and the problems entrenched. A club that is famed for its swagger has, in short, lost its mojo and the more you pull back the curtain, the longer it appears it will take to return. It would be oh so very typical of Harlequins to swashbuckle their way past Sale Sharks on Sunday but in many ways, that feels like part of the problem. During pre-season Harlequins set themselves the target of following in the footsteps of Exeter, who finished ninth two seasons ago before reaching the final last June . As Marcus Smith pointed out, it was not so long ago that Quins were seventh in January with only two wins and champions five months later .

summary_long: Billy B Van's 1919 comedy Van-ar-chy found by student in Sendai will be shown in early November in New Hampshire A silent comedy filmed in New Hampshire more than a century ago was recently found in Japan, and plans have been set to show the film in early November in the state where it was created. Van-ar-chy, a 1919 film starring the US entertainer and film-maker Billy B Van, was rediscovered by Kohei Okita, a film student in Sendai, Japan. While researching early cinema related to the word "anarchy", Okita bought several old film reels at an antique store in Japan and found the comedy starring Van, whom he did not recognize, according to a Van-ar-chy news release . summary_long: Diver Peter van Rodijnen's footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wilderness The North Sea, with its cold grey waters, is the world's drabbest. Or so you might have thought, but this documentary featuring the Dutch diver and underwater cinematographer Peter van Rodijnen sets out to tackle the misconceptions. His stunning footage puts all the splendours of this stormy stretch of water on show, and his voiceover gives it an endearing eccentric charm. First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea's waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. He also brings us cute, coo-worthy stories from the depths; take the male shorthorn sculpin fish (no looker, it must be said) who spends the winter looking after his eggs, cleaning and blowing fresh water over them. Van Rodijnen's camera is there for the baby fish hatching – pop, pop, pop out of their pearly plump pink eggs.

summary_long: A 'family' of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller In the last half-decade Stanley Tucci has been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightful cooking shows or smartly judged supporting turns in Conclave and The Devil Wears Prada 2 . He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one, Masterplan , sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related to Breathless star Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning in season two of Mike White's comedy). There's a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called "VR intrusion". As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. "I'm English," his character says at one point. "'Not bad' is what I say when I orgasm." Continue reading...

summary_long: With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee's There's no reason for anyone working on a new adaptation of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility to be intimidated by the celebrated 1995 movie by director Ang Lee and screenwriter Emma Thompson, any more than they should be or overawed by Austen's original novel. Sacred cows are there to be … not slain, but re-invented. The decision to bring out a next-gen Sense and Sensibility, with a new young cast – as opposed to, say, a new Northanger Abbey or a new spin on the unfinished The Watsons – might bemuse some and at first it bemused me, like hearing about a Love Actually remake starring Millie Bobby Brown. But this turns out to be a more downbeat, ruminative version, happening in much cloudier weather than 30 years ago and without the sugar-rush final wedding scene. The mood is cooler, but interestingly austere, sober and thoughtful. The sisters at the heart of the story, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, played in 1995 by Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, are now played by Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, and frankly don't look and sound much like the sisters we thought we knew. They look like young women who knew each other reasonably well at uni and are now in a flatshare in London.
